description: Ukrainian Favorite Recipe Cook Book Compiled and edited by Our Lady of Charity Guild at the  Saints Peter and Paul Ukrainian Catholic Church , Chisholm, Minnesota. 1962 (Revised) Edition. Acknowledgement :  "Our grateful and sincere thanks for the charitable cooperation of all our friends and neighbors (both near and far) who offered their cherished and favorite recipes, that others may share and enjoy them. Many of these are handed down, rare and unusual recipes that had often been asked for but were hard to find. Now they are gathered together for your convenience. We hope you like them.   – Our Lady of Charity Guild ------------------ The Saints Peter and Paul Ukrainian Catholic Church in Chisholm, Minnesota was built in 1916 by a congregation of Ukrainian immigrants and has played a significant role in the history of the Ukrainian community in Minnesota. It was listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1980 for its local significance in the themes of religion and social history, serving as a cornerstone for the Ukrainian American community, the final ethnic group to arrive on the Iron Range during its turn-of-the-20th-century immigration influx​. The onion dome tower on Central Ave. still catches the attention of those driving through town. The building is now a privately owned single-family dwelling.   The first Ukrainians arrived in Chisholm in the 1890s and took an active part in the building of the original community of Chisholm, which was incorporated as a village in 1901. These people came from such areas in Ukraine as Lisko and Sianok, in Western Galicia, and from around Uzhhorod, in the Carpathian region. The history of immigration to the area is not only typical of Ukrainians, but of non-Ukrainians as well, especially Slavs such as Croatians, Serbians, Slovaks, Slovenians, and others. Shortly after their arrival, the Ukrainian immigrants began formulating plans to construct their own church as a center of their religious and national activities.    Regarding the history of Ukrainian settlement in Minnesota , the Ukrainian community in Minneapolis began forming in the late 1870s when Ukrainians started emigrating from Eastern Europe to seek opportunities in the United States. Many Ukrainian immigrants initially settled in Northeast Minneapolis, which offered jobs and a low cost of living. This area became a welcoming place for Ukrainian immigrants, resulting in a population boom that led to the founding of Ukrainian businesses, social groups, and churches. The congregation of St. Constantine’s Ukrainian Catholic Church was established in 1913, and the congregation of St. Michael’s Ukrainian Orthodox Church formed in 1925​.   In the 1930s, Ukrainian Minnesotans launched cultural diplomacy efforts to raise funds and awareness in response to the Holodomor, a widespread famine in Ukraine that killed millions. These efforts included benefit musical performances by the Ukrainian National Chorus of the Twin Cities​. Following World War II, many Ukrainian refugees were recruited for jobs in the Twin Cities, with hundreds accepting the offer to move to Minnesota​. The Ukrainian community in Minneapolis also worked to preserve their cultural traditions, such as the making of pysanky, traditional Ukrainian Easter eggs​, and the opening of businesses that offered traditional Ukrainian foods​.   In the aftermath of political upheavals in Ukraine, such as the dissolution of the Soviet Union in 1991 and the invasion and annexation of Crimea by the Russian Federation in 2014, more Ukrainians migrated to Northeast Minneapolis. This trend continued into the 21st century, with Ukrainian Americans in Minneapolis remaining actively involved in efforts to provide relief and support for their home country​.

The Saints Peter and Paul Ukrainian Catholic Church in Chisholm, Minnesota was built in 1916 by a congregation of Ukrainian immigrants and has played a significant role in the history of the Ukrainian community in Minnesota. It was listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1980 for its local significance in the themes of religion and social history, serving as a cornerstone for the Ukrainian American community, the final ethnic group to arrive on the Iron Range during its turn-of-the-20th-century immigration influx​. The onion dome tower on Central Ave. still catches the attention of those driving through town. The building is now a privately owned single-family dwelling.

 

The first Ukrainians arrived in Chisholm in the 1890s and took an active part in the building of the original community of Chisholm, which was incorporated as a village in 1901. These people came from such areas in Ukraine as Lisko and Sianok, in Western Galicia, and from around Uzhhorod, in the Carpathian region. The history of immigration to the area is not only typical of Ukrainians, but of non-Ukrainians as well, especially Slavs such as Croatians, Serbians, Slovaks, Slovenians, and others. Shortly after their arrival, the Ukrainian immigrants began formulating plans to construct their own church as a center of their religious and national activities. 

 

Regarding the history of Ukrainian settlement in Minnesota, the Ukrainian community in Minneapolis began forming in the late 1870s when Ukrainians started emigrating from Eastern Europe to seek opportunities in the United States. Many Ukrainian immigrants initially settled in Northeast Minneapolis, which offered jobs and a low cost of living. This area became a welcoming place for Ukrainian immigrants, resulting in a population boom that led to the founding of Ukrainian businesses, social groups, and churches. The congregation of St. Constantine’s Ukrainian Catholic Church was established in 1913, and the congregation of St. Michael’s Ukrainian Orthodox Church formed in 1925​.

 

In the 1930s, Ukrainian Minnesotans launched cultural diplomacy efforts to raise funds and awareness in response to the Holodomor, a widespread famine in Ukraine that killed millions. These efforts included benefit musical performances by the Ukrainian National Chorus of the Twin Cities​. Following World War II, many Ukrainian refugees were recruited for jobs in the Twin Cities, with hundreds accepting the offer to move to Minnesota​. The Ukrainian community in Minneapolis also worked to preserve their cultural traditions, such as the making of pysanky, traditional Ukrainian Easter eggs​, and the opening of businesses that offered traditional Ukrainian foods​.

 

In the aftermath of political upheavals in Ukraine, such as the dissolution of the Soviet Union in 1991 and the invasion and annexation of Crimea by the Russian Federation in 2014, more Ukrainians migrated to Northeast Minneapolis. This trend continued into the 21st century, with Ukrainian Americans in Minneapolis remaining actively involved in efforts to provide relief and support for their home country​.
